I used to love going into my local music shop on Saturday morning and just hang out with all of the other various musicians who gathered there. I was usually trying out a new guitar that the shop had set out. We would swap stories and just hang out. It died in the late 90's. I hated to see it go. I'm sure he will be fine, though, because he has that "magic money". I bought a guitar off him one time and it had serious neck problems. I took it back to him and he said he was the greatest guitar tech in America, I kid you not. I came back later to pick up the guitar and all he did was crank the trem up. I'm doing what I can to keep it alive, 'booger. That's one of the many reasons why I keep the site going. I see the comments and the way people react to the articles, and see that they're things they never knew, never thought of, or never understood.

I may not be able to change the world, but I can do my part to try to preserve some of the important things - such as going to your local music store and actually learning and tying yourself into a network that wasn't some electronic social media network. It's also about supporting local businesses, helping our community (both the larger community and the community of musicians), and setting an example.

I actually use two "local" music shops. They're both pretty distant, with one being closer and down in Farmington (maybe an hour drive). The other is over in Fairfield and I stop at each of them, pretty much every time I'm in the area. Even if I only have a few minutes, I still stop in.

I generally leave with something - even if it's just strings, a strap, a new tuner, a new capo, or just picks.

I avoid the big box guitar stores like the plague - unless I have absolutely no choice. Fortunately, I don't have any of those near me. I think the closest is in Portland.

Sort of related, I love the smell of a music store. It's much like I like the smell of a bookstore, a farmer's union, or a small engine repair shop. At one point, after retiring, I seriously considered opening a music store with my specialty being vintage guitars and high-end products. Then, I realized that'd defeat the purpose of retiring.
